content: 1. Health and environmental risks associated with pesticides are classified according to internationally recognized systems such as those of the World Health Organization (WHO) or the Globally Harmonized System (GHS). These classifications may also be based on their inclusion in relevant binding international agreements or conventions. 2. Pesticides that are found to cause severe or irreversible harm to health or the environment under specific conditions of use in a country may be classified and treated as highly hazardous. 3. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) involves the careful evaluation of all available pest control methods and the subsequent integration of appropriate measures. These measures aim to discourage the development of pest populations while keeping pesticide use and other interventions at levels that are economically justified. IPM also seeks to minimize risks to human and animal health and the environment. 4. IPM prioritizes the cultivation of healthy crops with minimal disruption to agro-ecosystems and promotes natural pest control mechanisms. 5. Integrated Vector Management (IVM) refers to a rational decision-making process for the optimal use of resources in controlling disease vectors. It aims to enhance the efficacy, cost-effectiveness, ecological soundness, and sustainability of interventions for controlling vector-borne diseases. 6. An international organization refers to a public intergovernmental entity, including the United Nations (UN), UN Specialized Agencies and Programs, Development Banks, CGIAR Member Centers, and international scientific bodies such as IUPAC, CIPAC, and SETAC. 7. A label is the written, printed, or graphic information on or attached to a pesticide container, including the immediate container and any outer packaging or wrapper of the retail package. 8. The life cycle of a pesticide encompasses all stages from production to its degradation in the environment after use or its destruction as an unused product. This includes manufacturing, formulation, packaging, distribution, storage, transport, use, and final disposal of the pesticide and its container. 9. A manufacturer is any corporation or entity, whether public or private, engaged in the production of a pesticide active ingredient or its formulation, either directly or through an agent or contracted entity. 10. Marketing refers to the overall process of promoting a product, including advertising, public relations, information services, distribution, and sales in local or international markets. 11. Maximum Residue Limit (MRL) is the highest concentration of a pesticide residue legally permitted or recognized as acceptable in or on food, agricultural commodities, or animal feed. 12. Packaging refers to the container and protective wrapping used to transport pesticide products through wholesale or retail distribution to end users. 13. Personal protective equipment (PPE) includes any clothing, materials, or devices designed to protect individuals from pesticide exposure during handling and application. This includes both specially designed protective equipment and clothing reserved for pesticide use. 14. A pest is any species, strain, or biotype of plant, animal, or pathogenic agent that is harmful to plants, plant products, materials, or environments. This also includes vectors of parasites or pathogens of human and animal diseases, as well as animals causing public health nuisances. 15. A Pest Control Operator (PCO) is any individual or company that applies pesticides professionally. 16. A pesticide is any substance or mixture of substances, whether chemical or biological, intended to repel, destroy, or control pests or regulate plant growth. 17. Pesticide management involves the regulatory and technical oversight of all aspects of the pesticide life cycle, including production, authorization, import, distribution, sale, supply, transport, storage, handling, application, and disposal. The goal is to ensure safety, efficacy, and minimal adverse effects on health and the environment. 18. A poison is a substance capable of causing structural or functional disturbances, leading to illness, injury, or death when absorbed in relatively small amounts by humans, plants, or animals. 19. Poisoning refers to the occurrence of damage or disturbance caused by a poison, including intoxication. 20. A pesticide product refers to the formulated product, which includes the active ingredient(s) and co-formulants, in the form in which it is packaged and sold. 21. Product stewardship refers to the responsible and ethical management of a pesticide product throughout its entire life cycle, from discovery to ultimate use and beyond. 22. A public interest group includes, but is not limited to, scientific associations, farmer groups, citizens’ organizations, labor unions, and non-governmental environmental, consumer, and health organizations. 23. Public health uses of pesticides refer to pesticides employed in controlling pests of public health significance. These include disease vector control pesticides, household pesticide products, and professional pest control pesticides used in homes and public areas. 24. Registration is the process by which a national government or regional authority approves the sale and use of a pesticide after evaluating scientific data to demonstrate its effectiveness and ensure it does not pose unacceptable risks to human or animal health or the environment under the conditions of use in the country or region. 25. Repackaging involves transferring a pesticide from an authorized commercial package into another, usually smaller, container for subsequent sale. 26. Residue refers to any specified substances present in or on food, agricultural commodities, animal feed, or environmental media (soil, air, water) as a result of pesticide use. This includes derivatives such as conversion products, metabolites, breakdown products, reaction products, and impurities of toxicological or ecotoxicological significance. 27. A responsible authority is the government agency or agencies tasked with regulating pesticides and implementing pesticide legislation. 28. Risk is the probability and severity of an adverse health or environmental effect occurring as a function of a hazard and the likelihood and extent of exposure to a pesticide. 29. A severely restricted pesticide is one for which virtually all uses have been prohibited by final regulatory action to protect human health or the environment, except for certain specific uses that remain allowed. 30. Specification refers to the parameters and criteria defining the physical appearance and physical and chemical properties of technical and formulated pesticides, linked to their hazard and risk profiles. 31. A tender is a formal request for bids in the procurement of pesticides. 32. Toxicity is the physiological or biological property that determines a chemical’s capacity to cause harm or injury to a living organism by non-mechanical means. 33. A trader is anyone engaged in trade, including the export, import, and domestic distribution of pesticides. 34. Vulnerable groups include pregnant and nursing women, the unborn, infants and children, the elderly, individuals affected by HIV/AIDS, and workers or residents exposed to high levels of pesticides over the long term. 35. Governments bear the primary responsibility for regulating the availability, distribution, and use of pesticides within their countries and must allocate adequate resources to fulfill this mandate. 36. The pesticide industry should adhere to the provisions of this Code as a standard for the manufacture, distribution, sale, and advertising of pesticides, particularly in countries lacking effective regulatory schemes and advisory services. 37. Governments, industry, and other entities addressed by this Code should ensure compliance with relevant international agreements. 38. The pesticide industry and traders should follow best practices in pesticide management, especially in countries without adequate regulatory frameworks. 39. Entities involved in pesticide management should actively monitor their products throughout their life cycle, tracking major uses and addressing any problems that arise to determine the need for changes in labeling, usage directions, packaging, formulation, or product availability. 40. Pesticides requiring the use of personal protective equipment that is uncomfortable, expensive, or not readily available should be avoided, particularly for small-scale users and farmworkers in hot climates. 41. All relevant entities should collaborate to produce and disseminate clear educational materials on pesticide management through various media to extension services, agricultural and public health advisory services, farmers, pest control operators, and public health workers. 42. Users should be encouraged to seek educational materials and be supported in understanding and following the advice provided before handling and applying pesticides. 43. Governments should make concerted efforts to develop and promote the use of IPM and IVM. Lending institutions, donor agencies, and governments should support the development of national IPM/IVM policies and improved practices. 44. Stakeholders, including farmers, researchers, extension agents, crop consultants, the food industry, pesticide manufacturers, pest control operators, public health workers, environmentalists, and consumer representatives, should play an active role in promoting IPM/IVM. 45. Governments, with support from international and regional organizations, donor agencies, and research funds, should encourage research and development of alternatives to existing pesticides that pose fewer risks, such as biological control agents, non-chemical pesticides, and low-risk pesticides that degrade into harmless components after use. 46. Governments, the pesticide industry, and the application equipment industry should develop and promote pesticide application methods and equipment that minimize risks to health and the environment while optimizing efficiency and cost-effectiveness. Periodic practical training in these activities should also be conducted. 47. Governments, the pesticide industry, and national and international organizations should collaborate to develop strategies to prevent and manage pest resistance to pesticides, prolonging the useful life of valuable pesticides and reducing the adverse effects of resistance. 48. Countries with well-developed pesticide regulatory programs should provide technical assistance, including training, to other countries to help them build infrastructure and capacity for managing pesticides throughout their life cycle. 49. Countries should have access to facilities to verify and control the quality of pesticides offered for sale or export, ensuring compliance with FAO or WHO specifications or national standards. 50. International organizations and other interested bodies should assist in establishing or strengthening analytical laboratories in pesticide-importing countries, ensuring their economic and technical sustainability. 51. These laboratories should adhere to sound scientific procedures and guidelines for good laboratory practice and possess the necessary expertise.
